title: The Rocks

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA describes the asteroid field as 'a mineral wonderland!' The asteroids do not care about ARIA's enthusiasm.
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes asteroid mining is 'statistically one of the safer activities available to you.' From MARV, this is almost reassuring. Almost.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has armed the forward array. For mining. He insists the weapons lock is a 'mining configuration.' Nobody believes him.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that mineral yields from this field may qualify for the MineReward™ loyalty program! Redemption requires surviving the mining process!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY observes you could have hired a dedicated mining crew at the last station. But this is also a valid approach. A slower, riskier approach. But valid.

body:
An unremarkable asteroid field. The rocks drift slowly. The minerals are in there somewhere.

The ship computer notes that asteroid mining is 'statistically one of the safer activities available to you,' which says more about your other activities than about mining.

choices.text: Mine with the portable drill

outcome.narrative: The drill bites into rock. Minerals extracted. The drill was worth the cargo space. The ship computer logs the yield with something approaching satisfaction.

choices.text: Mine with standard equipment

outcome.narrative: Standard mining equipment works. Slowly. You extract minerals and some scrap. The computer notes the yield is 'adequate.' Back to adequate.

choices.text: Quick pass — grab what's easy and go

outcome.narrative: A quick pass yields scrap metal from the field's outer edge. Minimal effort, minimal reward. The rocks don't mind.

choices.text: Skip — save time, move on

outcome.narrative: You pass through the field without stopping. The rocks continue to drift. They will be here when the next ship comes. Or they won't. Rocks are unpredictable on geological timescales.

title: The Contested Claim

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is sure the other ship is friendly! Most ships are friendly! She has no data to support this!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has identified the other ship. It is not friendly. He will let events confirm this.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has locked weapons. This is technically the correct response. REX is gratified.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that claim disputes are covered under Section 14 of the Mining Rights Act. The other ship does not appear to have read Section 14.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes you could have checked the claim registry before entering the field. It's public information. Just saying.

body:
The asteroid field has a faded corporate mining claim staked on the largest rock. The claim expired six months ago. Mining it is technically legal.

A ship on long-range sensors suggests someone disagrees about the 'technically' part.

choices.text: Mine fast — grab what you can before they arrive

outcome.narrative: You mined fast. The other ship arrived as you were leaving. They hailed you. You did not answer. The minerals are in your hold. The moral high ground is not.

choices.text: Negotiate — explain the claim expired

outcome.narrative: Your diplomat explained the legal situation. The other captain listened. There was a long pause. Then they proposed splitting the field. You got the better half. Diplomacy works. Occasionally.

choices.text: Leave — not worth the confrontation

outcome.narrative: You left the field. The other ship did not pursue. The minerals remain in their rocks. The rocks remain in their field. Nothing changed except your fuel reserves.

title: Claim Jumper's Dilemma

ai_flavor.aria: An abandoned mining rig! Finders keepers is a real law, right? ARIA is asking! ARIA genuinely does not know!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the claim registry. The claim expired eight years ago. The claimant's renewal notice is still taped to the rig. MARV finds the tape more binding than the law.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has secured the rig. It was not resisting. He notes prior tenants left in a hurry: half a meal, one boot. He does not speculate about the boot. Out loud.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP confirms the claim is legally lapsed! Salvage rights apply! CHIP loves it when the law and the loot agree!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the rig's drill head is worth more than everything else on it combined, and that removing it properly takes six careful hours, and that improperly takes one exciting one.

body:
An automated mining rig clings to the largest rock in the cluster, dark and pitted, drill head buried mid-bite. The claim beacon still transmits, faithfully, a claim that expired eight years ago.

Someone sank real money into this rig and then stopped coming back for it. The rocks don't know why. The registry doesn't say. The rig just waits, holding its last bite of asteroid like a dog nobody came home to.

choices.text: Strip the rig for materials

outcome.narrative: Six hours of honest disassembly. The rig comes apart into metal stock, scrap, and one beautifully preserved drive coil. The claim beacon is left transmitting on its little backup cell — it seemed wrong to silence it. It'll outlast everyone involved in this decision.

choices.text: Restart the rig and take one load

outcome.narrative: The engineer coaxes the old rig through one last shift. It drills like it never stopped — eight hours, one full hopper of ore, and a shutdown sequence it performs with what reads as relief. You bank the load and power it down properly, the way somebody should have, eight years ago.

choices.text: Check the habitation pod first

outcome.narrative: The pod tells a short story: half a meal, one boot, a departure faster than boots. And on the console, a note, handwritten: 'Gone to flag down the med-ship. Rig's yours if I'm not back. —K.' Eight years. You take nothing. The claim beacon transmits all the way out of sensor range.

choices.text: Check the logbook: it mentions this rig

outcome.narrative: The logbook has a page on this rig. Its author met the owner, K, eight years ago: tired, friendly, coughing, waiting on a med-ship that was late. K gave them the restart code 'in case'. It still works. The rig runs one last shift and you bank the ore. In the habitation pod, under a coffee ring, a note in K's hand says what the logbook says: gone to flag down the med-ship.

choices.text: Respect the claim and move on

outcome.narrative: Expired or not, it's somebody's rig. You log its position for the registry — 'equipment intact, claimant absent' — and leave it holding its bite of rock. The law had an opinion. The tape on the renewal notice had a better one.

science_link.text: MARV notes that mining rocks like these is a real proposal, with real math, and realer skepticism.
science_link.label: Asteroid mining, seriously proposed

title: The Singing Rock

ai_flavor.aria: One of the asteroids is HUMMING! ARIA has matched the pitch! They're in harmony now! This is the best field ever!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies the hum as piezoelectric resonance from compressed quartz veins. He delivers this explanation to a crew that has clearly already decided it's magic. He logs 'magic (piezoelectric).'
ai_flavor.rex: REX confirmed the humming rock is not a beacon, a lure, or a mine. It is a rock, humming. He has filed it under 'no action required' with unusual reluctance.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that novelty audio recordings sell well at stations! The rock's performance is unlicensed! The rock cannot sign! CHIP sees an opportunity in that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has recorded forty minutes of the hum. Played at half speed, she notes, it resolves into something very like a chord progression. She is not going to play it at half speed again.

body:
One of the asteroids is humming.

A low, steady tone, right at the edge of the sensors' hearing — solar heat working a quartz vein, physics doing an impression of a voice. The tone rises a little as the rock turns its face to the star, and falls as it turns away. Sunrise and sunset, rendered as a note.

The crew has been listening on the open channel for twenty minutes. Nobody has suggested moving on. You are, technically, behind schedule. The rock is, technically, singing.

choices.text: Drift alongside and listen a while

outcome.narrative: You match the rock's slow tumble and let it sing to the hull for an hour. No analysis, no sampling, no yield. Days later, crew members are still humming the note while they work — the field's one song, carried on in five imperfect covers.

choices.text: Core a sample of the quartz

outcome.narrative: The drill takes a clean core of the singing vein. The tone drops a quarter-step and does not recover. The sample is scientifically excellent and worth real money, and the away team returns quieter than they left. Fair trade is a matter of ongoing internal debate.

choices.text: Record it for the ship's library

outcome.narrative: Forty minutes of asteroid, recorded clean, filed in the ship's library between the emergency drills and someone's audiobooks. It becomes the unofficial soundtrack of third watch. The rock, uncredited, achieves the widest audience of its four-billion-year career.

science_link.text: MARV files the explanation for the singing: compressed quartz making electricity. The effect is real, and it is called piezoelectricity.
science_link.label: Piezoelectricity: rocks that sing

title: The Shoal

ai_flavor.aria: Look at them all moving together! It's like a school of fish! Fish are friendly! These are rocks, but in spirit!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has modelled the shoal. Three thousand bodies, most of them small, all of them turning. He has found a line through. He notes the line is narrowing at a rate he would describe, if pressed, as brisk.
ai_flavor.rex: REX counts three thousand inbound contacts and zero hostiles. He finds the zero unconvincing. Point defense is warm. Point defense will not help.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Collision Waiver covers impacts with up to one (1) object per voyage! You are about to exceed it! CHIP has pre-filed the paperwork!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY would go around. It costs fuel and days and nobody gets a story out of it. She's fine without the story.

body:
A shoal of rocks has drifted across your heading: a few thousand of them, none bigger than a house, all of them turning. They move together, the way fish do, for reasons that are entirely gravitational and look entirely deliberate.

There is a gap through the middle. It is closing. Most of the rocks are small. Small, at these speeds, is a relative term.

choices.text: Thread the gap at speed

outcome.narrative: You aim at the gap and go. The gap is narrower at the far end than it looked from the near one, which is how gaps work. Twelve points of hull, and one rock the size of a fist straight through the water tank, in a bang that everyone aboard will describe differently for the rest of their lives. Six points of water leave by the new hole before it is plugged.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} picks a line through

outcome.narrative: The pilot slows to a crawl and takes the shoal rock by rock, matching the tumble, never quite touching. Two days. Six points of fuel. One gentle scrape, which the pilot apologises to the ship for, out loud.

choices.text: Back out and go around

outcome.narrative: You turn and fly the long way round the shoal, which is very long, because the shoal is very wide. Four days, ten points of fuel and six of food. Not one rock touches the ship. Dinner is smaller every night and nobody has anything to say about it, which was the point.

choices.text: Shields up and ride it out

outcome.narrative: You take the shield console and point the ship at the gap.

perfect.narrative: You hold the shields through the thick of it, easing off between impacts and slamming them up on every flash. Three points of hull, all of it scuffs. The shoal closes behind you like a door.

good.narrative: The shields take most of it. Most is not all: seven points of hull got through in the seconds you were catching your breath, and one of them found the water tank, which lost three more. The shoal closes behind you, unbothered.

poor.narrative: The shields drop mid-shoal. The rest of the crossing happens to the hull directly, at length: sixteen points of it, and a split seam in the water tank that weeps six more before anyone finds it. The crew spends the evening listening to the ship tick as it cools, counting.

title: The Rock Exhales

ai_flavor.aria: The asteroid is breathing! ARIA always knew rocks had feelings! It is a very big breath! She is sure it will finish soon!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the pocket held four billion years of frozen gas. He estimates it will finish venting at about the moment the spin becomes a problem. He has started a clock. He did not want to.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has identified the asteroid as the aggressor. It fired first. It is still firing. He recommends disengaging from the asteroid, a sentence he never expected to say.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the anchor cable is rental equipment! Cutting it incurs a Non-Return Fee! CHIP will add it to the invoice! The invoice is getting long!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has her hand on the cable release. She isn't pulling it. She's just making it very clear that it's there.

body:
The anchor bit into the asteroid at 0400. At 0412 the asteroid exhaled.

Under the anchor point there was a pocket of frozen gas that had waited four billion years for someone to put a hole in it, and it has opinions. A white plume is venting past the hull, and the ship, still tethered, is beginning to turn with the rock. Slowly. Then less slowly.

choices.text: Cut the cable and burn clear

outcome.narrative: The cable goes with a twang you feel in your teeth, and you burn clear before the spin takes hold. Twelve points of fuel. The anchor stays in the rock, which now has a small monument to you sticking out of it. Nobody suggests going back for it.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} vents it down the drill shaft

outcome.narrative: The engineer feeds the plume back down the drill shaft and throttles it with a valve that was not designed for this and does it anyway. The spin stops. The shaft coughs up a load of loose ore on its way. The airlock cycled four times getting them in and out, and holding the ship steady while they worked burned a little fuel.

choices.text: Ride the spin until it runs out

outcome.narrative: You hold on. Everyone holds on. The spin climbs for an hour and then, as the pocket empties, winds down for another two, the tether groaning the whole time. Somebody lost their grip in the second hour and met a bulkhead. The galley lockers lost theirs in the first, and a week of stores went round the walls along with everyone's lunch.

choices.text: Cap the vent with a hull patch

outcome.narrative: You slap the patch over the vent, sticky side down, instructions side up. It holds. The rock goes quiet and stays quiet, wearing a small square of the ship's stores that will outlast everyone aboard. A little air got out while you worked.

title: Collision Cascade

ai_flavor.aria: Two asteroids met! And now there are thousands of little asteroids! That's how families work! ARIA is so happy for them!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV watched the collision. He has modelled the debris front. It expands at a rate he has written down and underlined twice. He notes that a cascade does not end. It only thins.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports the largest coordinated inbound assault of his career. Thousands of projectiles. No command structure. No demands. He respects it. He would like to leave.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Impact Protection™ is priced per impact! CHIP has done the arithmetic! CHIP recommends declaring bankruptcy now, while it's affordable!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has the scanner on wide sweep. There will be holes in that cloud and somebody has to find them fast. She'd rather it was a person than luck.

body:
Two rocks the size of cities have met, a few thousand kilometers ahead, at a speed neither of them had planned for. There was no sound. There will be no sound. There is, instead, a cloud: a sphere of everything they were, expanding at several kilometers a second, and the ship is inside the radius it will reach in about twenty minutes.

The cloud is mostly gaps. The gaps are moving too.

choices.text: Scan for the gaps and fly them

outcome.narrative: You take the scanner and look for holes.

perfect.narrative: You lock onto the gaps one after another and call the turns, and the ship slips through the front in a run of hard, sickening swerves. Three points of hull, four of fuel. Behind you the cloud keeps going, and will for a long time.

good.narrative: You find most of the gaps. The ones you miss find the ship instead: ten points of hull, most of it in one long, loud second near the end.

poor.narrative: The scanner loses the gaps halfway through and the ship goes through the front blind. Twenty-two points of hull. Everyone aboard can now say, accurately, that they were caught in an asteroid collision. Nobody wants to.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} turns the cargo doors into a shield

outcome.narrative: The engineer unbolts the cargo doors, swings them out on the crane arms and angles them into the front like two very expensive umbrellas. The debris hits the doors, which is the idea. Eight points of hull get round the edges. With enough hands the doors go back on quickly; without them, it is days of hammering.

choices.text: Hide behind the biggest fragment

outcome.narrative: You tuck in behind the largest piece of what used to be a city-sized rock and let it take the front. It takes the front. It also spins, which nobody had fully thought about, and the ship spends four days dodging its own shelter. Eight points of fuel, ten of hull.

choices.text: Turn back the way you came

outcome.narrative: You turn round and burn hard back down your own track, then round the edge of the front the very long way. Four days. The cloud never catches you. The fuel gauge does: a third of the tank, gone into running away.

choices.text: Punch straight through the front

outcome.narrative: You aim for the middle and go through at full speed, on the theory that less time inside is less time being hit. The theory is half right. Twenty-eight points of hull, and one fragment that came through the plating into a cabin that was occupied.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference: collisions that make debris that makes more collisions have a name, and the people who keep satellites flying around Earth worry about it a great deal.
science_link.label: Collision cascades
